reason: The sources provide over 15 cross-referenced facts supported by at least two distinct sites, creating a compelling 45-second script about Polaris's multi-star nature and celestial movement.
story: Many people believe the North Star, Polaris, is the brightest star in the night sky, but it actually ranks only around 47th or 48th. Its fame comes from standing nearly motionless above Earth's North Pole, anchored by Earth's rotational axis while other stars appear to circle it. But Polaris holds an even bigger secret: it is not a single star. It is a triple star system dominated by Polaris Aa, a yellow supergiant more than two thousand times brighter than our Sun. Orbiting close to it every thirty years is a smaller companion star, Polaris Ab, which was directly photographed for the first time by the Hubble Space Telescope. A third companion, Polaris B, orbits much farther out and was discovered by William Herschel in 1779. Due to Earth's 26,000-year axial precession, Polaris will not remain our North Star forever; by 4000 AD, Gamma Cephei will take its place.
angle: The iconic North Star isn't a single star and isn't the brightest star in the sky—it's a triple star system dominated by a yellow supergiant thousands of times more luminous than the Sun.

claims.claim: Polaris is not the brightest star in the night sky, ranking around 47th or 48th in apparent magnitude.
Polaris is actually a triple star system composed of three stars.
Polaris marks the north celestial pole because it is located nearly in line with Earth's rotational axis above the North Pole.
Polaris appears virtually stationary in the sky while other northern stars appear to rotate around it.
Earth's axial precession causes the celestial pole to wobble in a cycle lasting approximately 26,000 years.
Polaris will make its closest approach to the north celestial pole around the year 2100 to 2105.
Around 4000 AD, the star Errai (Gamma Cephei) will replace Polaris as Earth's North Star.
Polaris is the closest Cepheid variable star to Earth.
Polaris is located in the constellation Ursa Minor and marks the end of the handle of the Little Dipper.
The Hubble Space Telescope was used to directly image the close inner companion star Polaris Ab for the first time.
The primary star Polaris Aa is an evolved yellow supergiant.
The inner companion Polaris Ab orbits the primary star with a period of roughly 30 years.
The outer companion Polaris B was discovered by William Herschel in August 1779.
The elevation of Polaris above the horizon directly corresponds to the observer's geographic latitude.
Stargazers can locate Polaris by following a line through the pointer stars Dubhe and Merak in the Big Dipper.
Polaris is situated between 430 and 446 light-years from Earth.
Polaris Aa is more than two thousand times more luminous than our Sun.
The mass of the close companion Polaris Ab is approximately 1.25 to 1.3 times the mass of the Sun.

disputed: Exact distance to Polaris (older models state ~430 light-years, Hipparcos states ~432 light-years, Gaia DR3 states ~446.5 light-years, while disputed short-distance models suggested ~323 light-years): attribute by citing modern space telescopes like Gaia or giving a general range of 430–446 light-years.
Exact mass of Polaris Aa (estimates range from 4.3 to 5.4 solar masses depending on measurement method and orbit models): frame as roughly 4.5 to 5.4 solar masses.
Pulsation mode of Polaris Aa (whether it is a fundamental or first-overtone pulsator): attribute as a subject of ongoing stellar evolution research if mentioned.
